steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a database/PL paper on adaptive optimization of recursive queries. It should motivate why recursive queries are hard to optimize, cover Datalog and adaptive query processing, and introduce our technique (Adaptive Metaprogramming) and our system Carac, ending with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: recursion is back in analytical queries, optimization lags
- Why SQL systems struggle with recursive queries
- Datalog as the alternative and its limits
- Adaptive query processing and code generation, and why they fall short
- Our approach: Adaptive Metaprogramming in Carac
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - advanced algorithms need more expressive queries than relational algebra (iterative / fixed-point)
  - resurgence of recursion in analytical queries
  - recursive query optimization lags behind non-recursive
- SQL and recursion
  - recursion added in ANSI’99 SQL standard
  - most relational systems not optimized for it
  - results of current iteration fed into next iteration
  - cardinalities change unpredictably; number of iterations unknown ahead of time
  - cardinality estimation assumes fixed input cardinalities -> no good join orders after first iteration
- Datalog
  - developers turn to Datalog for high-performance recursion
  - used for: Java program analysis, TensorFlow, Ethereum Virtual Machine, AWS network analysis
  - bottom-up evaluation: unions of conjunctive queries applied repeatedly
  - state-of-the-art engines: manual or offline join-order optimization, need profiling, can't adapt to real-time data
- AQP + code generation
  - AQP uses runtime info, avoids error-prone cardinality estimation
  - code-generating systems: partially evaluate plans into compiled executables, avoid interpretation overhead
  - but code-generating AQP doesn't recompile at runtime; jumps between precompiled plans/code blocks (optimizing compiler too expensive)
  - recursive queries: optimal plan doesn't stay optimal; too many paths to enumerate/compile ahead-of-time
  - need: optimization using runtime info for recursive queries
- Our approach
  - Adaptive Metaprogramming: runtime optimization and repeated re-optimization of recursive queries
  - Carac: specialized Datalog engine tightly integrated with general-purpose language
  - uses Multi-Stage Programming (known PL technique) for runtime code generation
  - goal: show an approach any recursive engine could use to continuously reapply optimizations
- Contributions
  - Adaptive Metaprogramming = code-generating JIT data systems + Multi-Stage Programming, regenerates code at runtime
  - custom Datalog join-order optimization from ahead-of-time to just-in-time (runtime stats like cardinalities)
  - Carac results: over 5000x vs unoptimized, 6x vs hand-optimized

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Modern applications run advanced algorithms that need query capabilities that are more expressive than traditional relational algebra, for example iterative or fixed-point computations. Because of this, recursion is being used again in analytical queries. But recursive query optimization techniques have not been developed as much as the ones for non-recursive queries.

Recursion support was added to the SQL standard in ANSI’99, but most relational data management systems are still not optimized for what recursive queries need. When a recursive query runs, the relations that result from the current iteration are fed as input into the next iteration of query evaluation. This means the relation cardinalities can change in ways that are hard to predict, and the number of iterations needed to run the query is not known ahead of time. Existing cardinality estimation techniques assume that input relation cardinalities do not change during execution, so they can't guarantee good join orders after the first iteration.

So developers use Datalog instead for high-performance recursive query processing. Datalog is a popular query language for recursive queries and it has been used for Java program analysis, TensorFlow, the Ethereum Virtual Machine, AWS network analysis, and other applications where performance is critical. Most Datalog engines use bottom-up evaluation, where subqueries that are unions of conjunctive queries get applied to relations again and again. State-of-the-art Datalog engines offer manual or offline join-order optimizations for these subqueries, but they need a profiling stage and they cannot adapt when the real-time data is different from what was profiled.

  - code-generating systems compile plans, avoid interpretation overhead
  - but no runtime recompilation; jump between precompiled plans (optimizing compiler too expensive)
  - recursive queries: optimal plan doesn't stay optimal; too many paths to compile ahead-of-time
  - need optimization using runtime info for recursive queries
- Our approach: Adaptive Metaprogramming, Carac (Datalog engine + general-purpose language, Multi-Stage Programming for runtime code generation)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Modern applications run advanced algorithms that need query capabilities that are more expressive than traditional relational algebra, for example iterative or fixed-point computations. Because of this, recursion is being used again in analytical queries. But recursive query optimization techniques have not been developed as much as the ones for non-recursive queries.

Recursion support was added to the SQL standard in ANSI’99, but most relational data management systems are still not optimized for what recursive queries need. When a recursive query runs, the relations that result from the current iteration are fed as input into the next iteration of query evaluation. This means the relation cardinalities can change in ways that are hard to predict, and the number of iterations needed to run the query is not known ahead of time. Existing cardinality estimation techniques assume that input relation cardinalities do not change during execution, so they can't guarantee good join orders after the first iteration.

So developers use Datalog instead for high-performance recursive query processing. Datalog is a popular query language for recursive queries and it has been used for Java program analysis, TensorFlow, the Ethereum Virtual Machine, AWS network analysis, and other applications where performance is critical. Most Datalog engines use bottom-up evaluation, where subqueries that are unions of conjunctive queries get applied to relations again and again. State-of-the-art Datalog engines offer manual or offline join-order optimizations for these subqueries, but they need a profiling stage and they cannot adapt when the real-time data is different from what was profiled.

Cardinality estimation is error-prone, so adaptive query processing (AQP) avoids it by using runtime information to tune query optimization. AQP can be combined with code-generating data management systems, which partially evaluate query plans into compiled executables so there is no interpretation overhead, and this improves query execution performance. But code-generating AQP systems do not regenerate and compile code at runtime. They jump between precompiled plans or code blocks instead, because invoking an optimizing compiler during query execution costs too much. Recursive queries execute subqueries over and over and the results of one iteration go into the next, so an optimal query plan does not stay optimal for the whole execution of a single program, and there are too many possible paths to enumerate or compile ahead-of-time. So we need query optimization techniques that can use runtime information and that meet the specific optimization criteria of recursive query processing.

In this work we introduce Adaptive Metaprogramming to address these challenges. It is a new technique for runtime optimization and repeated re-optimization of recursive queries. We implement and evaluate the design in Carac. Carac is a system that tightly integrates a specialized Datalog execution engine with a general-purpose programming language, and it uses Multi-Stage Programming, a known technique from the Programming Languages community, to support runtime code generation. In the end the goal of Carac is to show a new optimization approach that uses advanced metaprogramming language capabilities, which would let any recursive query processing engine keep reapplying optimizations. The contributions of this paper are:

- We introduce Adaptive Metaprogramming, a technique that combines code-generating just-in-time data management systems with Multi-Stage Programming. This enables adaptive, continuous query re-optimization by regenerating code at runtime.

- We use Adaptive Metaprogramming for a custom optimization for Datalog queries that selects efficient join orders of conjunctive subqueries at different stages in the lifetime of the query, from ahead-of-time, when only the queries are available, to just-in-time, when runtime statistics like relation cardinalities are available.

- With our custom Datalog engine Carac, we show that Adaptive Metaprogramming can speed up unoptimized Datalog queries by over 5000x and still keep a 6x speedup over manually hand-optimized queries.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The advanced algorithms that power contemporary applications require query capabilities more expressive than traditional relational algebra, for example iterative or fixed-point computations. This demand has led to a resurgence of recursion in analytical queries, yet recursive query optimization techniques lag behind those established for non-recursive queries.

Support for recursion was added to the ANSI’99 SQL standard, yet most relational data management systems are not optimized for the specific needs of recursive queries: during execution of a recursive query, the relations resulting from the current iteration are fed as input into the next iteration of query evaluation. As a result, relation cardinalities can change unpredictably and the number of iterations needed to execute the query is not known ahead of time. Existing cardinality estimation techniques assume that input relation cardinalities do not change during execution, and so cannot guarantee high-quality join orders after the first iteration.

Instead, developers turn to Datalog for high-performance recursive query processing. Datalog is a popular query language for recursive queries that has been used for Java program analysis [1], TensorFlow [2], Ethereum Virtual Machine [3], AWS network analysis [4], and other performance-critical applications. Most Datalog engines follow a bottom-up evaluation [5] strategy, in which subqueries in the form of unions of conjunctive queries are repeatedly applied to relations. State-of-the-art Datalog engines provide manual or offline join-order optimizations for these subqueries, but they require a profiling stage and cannot adapt if the real-time data does not match what was profiled.

To avoid error-prone cardinality estimation [6], adaptive query processing (AQP) uses runtime information to tune query optimization [7]. This can be combined with code-generating data management systems [8,9,10], which improve query execution performance by partially evaluating query plans into compiled executables and so avoiding interpretation overhead. However, code-generating AQP systems do not regenerate and compile code at runtime; they jump between precompiled plans or code blocks to avoid the prohibitively high cost of invoking an optimizing compiler during query execution [11,12]. Because recursive queries repeatedly execute subqueries whose results from the previous iteration feed the next, an optimal query plan will not stay optimal over the execution of a single program, and the number of potential paths is too large to enumerate or compile ahead-of-time. There is thus a need for query optimization techniques that leverage runtime information to meet the specific optimization criteria of recursive query processing.

To address these challenges, this work introduces Adaptive Metaprogramming, a novel technique for runtime optimization and repeated re-optimization of recursive queries. We implement and evaluate the design in Carac, a system that tightly integrates a specialized Datalog execution engine with a general-purpose programming language and uses Multi-Stage Programming [13], a known technique from the Programming Languages community, to support runtime code generation. Ultimately, Carac aims to illustrate a novel optimization approach that leverages advanced metaprogramming language capabilities, which would enable any recursive query processing engine to continuously reapply optimizations. This paper makes the following contributions:

- We introduce Adaptive Metaprogramming, a technique that combines code-generating just-in-time data management systems with Multi-Stage Programming to enable adaptive, continuous query re-optimization by regenerating code at runtime.

- We use Adaptive Metaprogramming to enable a custom optimization for Datalog queries that selects efficient join orders of conjunctive subqueries at different stages of the query's lifetime: from ahead-of-time, when only queries are available, to just-in-time, when runtime statistics such as relation cardinalities are available.

- Through our custom Datalog engine Carac, we show that Adaptive Metaprogramming can speed up unoptimized Datalog queries by over 5000x while maintaining a 6x speedup over manually hand-optimized queries.
